idiom_name: sync.Mutex field with published Lock()/Unlock() (sync.Locker) on pointer receivers
implementation_notes: Go's standard library supplies both the primitive and the interface: sync.Mutex lives as a struct field, sync.Locker is the published Lock()/Unlock() pair, and a locked mutex is not associated with a goroutine - one goroutine may lock and another may unlock - so the published-lock shape is mechanically supported. Enforcement is missing, however: there is no reentrancy, no owner tracking and no guard type, so the discipline is documentation plus runtime traps. A Mutex must not be copied after first use (the package doc says values containing these types should not be copied, and go vet's copylocks analyzer flags copies because both copies then malfunction), every method must take a pointer receiver, and embedding sync.Mutex would promote Lock/Unlock into the public API unintentionally - prefer a private mutex with critical-section methods, and publish the lock explicitly only when callers need compound atomicity.
pitfalls: Copying an Account (passing it by value, storing it in a slice of structs, ranging over Accounts) copies the mutex; go vet's copylocks analyzer reports it and each copy then guards a different state.

sync.Mutex is not reentrant, and methods that lock the same mutex cannot be called while the caller already holds it - document that a held lock admits no re-entrant calls, or split internal unlocked helpers.
There is no guard and no owner: a missing Unlock on an early return leaks the lock, and any goroutine may unlock (misuse surfaces as a panic only when nothing holds the mutex).
The stdlib notes that TryLock uses are rare and often a sign of a deeper problem; prefer blocking acquisition, and express bounded waiting with contexts and channels instead of spinning.
